Base directory for this skill: /work/.claude/skills/jigc

`jigc setup` wrote this file from jigc 1.0.0-rc.11 and owns it: re-run `jigc setup` after upgrading the binary to refresh it.

It carries the two guides that ship with that binary, one after the other — the quickstart loop, then the migration field notes. A cross-reference to `QUICKSTART.md` or `MIGRATING.md` means the matching part of this file; every other jigc document named below lives in the jigc project's own repository, not in this one, which is why none of them are links here.

# Quickstart

`jigc` is a context compiler for coding agents: a deterministic CLI that
assembles exactly the instructions and document slices an agent needs for a
task, and is the sole channel through which the agent reads and writes managed
project documents. This walks the MVP loop on a real machine —
**install → start → finalize**.

> The name is **jigc** — pronounced "jig-see" — *a jig for coding agents*: the
> jig holds the work and guides the tool so the cut lands true (settled
> 2026-07-03, `DECISIONS.md` → The name is settled). The binary is the same name.

## Install

`jigc` ships as a single binary. Install it from the workspace and put it on
your `PATH`:

```sh
cargo install --path crates/cli      # or: cargo build --release -p cli
cp target/release/jigc /usr/local/bin/   # if you built rather than installed
```

Just `jigc` — nothing else to copy. The doc↔code probe (`doc-code`) is
embedded in the binary and extracted beside it by `jigc setup` (below), so a
`cargo install` from a fresh machine is a supported install channel: no manual
probe copy, and code-anchor finalize / `jigc validate` work out of the box.

Confirm it identifies itself:

```sh
jigc --version          # → jigc <version>
```

## 1. `jigc setup` — adapter install

Run once per project, from the repo root. `setup` generates the Claude Code
adapter from the embedded profile and installs it idempotently
(`design/assistant-adapter.md` → Generated, minimal, regenerated):

```sh
jigc setup
```

It does these things:

- writes the managed bootstrap file `.jigc/AGENT.md` and adds a bare
  `@.jigc/AGENT.md` import to `CLAUDE.md` (the static floor that tells the agent
  `jigc` is its interface to the project — a plain import line, no marker fence);
- allowlists `Bash(jigc:*)` in `.claude/settings.json` and adds a `SessionStart` hook
  that runs `jigc start` (so each session opens with orientation), so the agent
  can call the CLI without a permission prompt;
- writes jigc's own guides — this file and the migration field notes — to the path
  your assistant reads skills from (`.claude/skills/jigc/SKILL.md` for Claude Code),
  as **one file jigc owns**: it opens with a `jigc-version:` stamp naming the build
  that wrote it plus the hash of its own body, and every `jigc setup` rewrites it, so
  the guidance in your repo always matches the binary in your `PATH`. Re-run `setup`
  after upgrading and the copy follows;
- extracts the embedded `doc-code` probe beside the installed `jigc` (so the
  doc↔code probe resolves next to the binary — written if no sibling is present
  **or** if an existing sibling's bytes differ from the embedded copy, so a
  stale or corrupt probe self-heals; a byte-identical sibling is left untouched); and
- installs a `pre-commit` hook that runs `jigc validate` over the committed
  store and **warns** on doc↔code drift without blocking the commit — a
  backstop for edits made outside the loop, not a gate. It refuses exactly one
  thing: a commit that itself stages an out-of-band managed-doc **rename** (a
  bare `git mv` of a managed doc, both paths staged), because that silently
  breaks identity tracking — use `jigc rename` instead. Drift that landed in an
  earlier commit only warns; it never blocks a later, unrelated one.

`setup` **commits its own install** as a dedicated
`chore(jigc): install jigc workspace config` commit, so the install doesn't land in
your first feature commit. It stages **only the files it wrote inside the repo** —
never your working tree — so two of the things above are *not* in that commit: the
`doc-code` probe (it lives beside the `jigc` binary, not in your repo), and the
`pre-commit` hook whenever git keeps hooks outside your working tree — the usual
`.git/hooks/`, a `core.hooksPath` pointing elsewhere, or a linked worktree's shared
hooks dir — because git cannot track a file there. If your repo keeps hooks *in* the
tree (an in-repo `core.hooksPath`), the hook is an ordinary tracked file and `setup`
commits it with the rest — unless git will not take that path from your repo, in which
case `setup` leaves the hook out of its commit and commits the rest normally. That
covers a hooks dir belonging to **another** repository (shared hooks vendored as a
submodule — checked out or not — or an embedded repo), where it is that repo's file to
commit, not yours, and a hooks dir your **sparse-checkout** excludes. Either way the
hook is installed and works locally, it just isn't in the commit; note that a committed
hook carries **this** machine's `jigc`
path, so in someone else's clone it stays silent until they run `jigc setup`
themselves. These edits are idempotent — re-running `jigc setup` leaves the files
byte-identical (no new commit), so it is safe to run after every upgrade to re-apply
the adapter.

## 2. `jigc start "<intent>"` — route, then mint

Hand the agent (or yourself) a task by stating the intent. `start` composes
the cascade-default **router** (`design/write-commands.md` → Task
origination): it presents the selectable work-workflows with the situation
each fits, and emits the re-run line — nothing is minted yet:

```sh
jigc start "add per-client rate limit at the gateway"
# → the workflow menu, then the re-run line:
#   jigc start --workflow <chosen> "<intent>"
```

Pick the workflow whose situation fits the intent and re-run with that
choice — this is the call that mints:

```sh
jigc start --workflow single-task "add per-client rate limit at the gateway"
```

This opens the task's working area under `.jigc/tasks/<id>/` and emits the
composed workflow — the instructions plus the document slices the task needs.
The agent reads its intent and the codebase, implements the change directly in
the working tree, and (when a decision is warranted) records an ADR in-task
through the workflow's `create` gate.

Bare `jigc start` (no intent) orients instead: it reports project state and the
next action, read-only.

## 3. `jigc task finalize <id>` — the commit boundary

When the work is done, finalize. This is the single transactional boundary
(`design/finalize.md`): it validates, renders the commit-doc into the git commit
message, promotes any created ADR into `docs/decisions/`, and `git`-commits the
code changes plus promoted docs as one commit.

```sh
jigc task finalize <id>
```

If validation blocks (a dangling forward reference, a missing required slot, a
malformed value), finalize makes no commit and surfaces the findings with a
route for the next action. Fix and re-run.

Your own `pre-commit` / `commit-msg` hooks still run — jigc never passes
`--no-verify`, they are your policy — so a hook that rejects the commit stops
the finalize. Nothing is committed, the task survives with your staged set
still staged, and the message carries the hook's own output verbatim plus the
line to re-run once its complaint is fixed. Every jigc verb that commits on
your behalf answers a rejection that way, each stating what *its* rejection
left behind — the per-door detail is in MIGRATING.md →
Reconciling and backing out.

A landed finalize prints a **manifest** — the file-set the commit carried (the
git index: what you staged plus the docs jigc promotes), with a distinct
**left-out** list naming any unstaged or untracked work the commit excluded (so
a stray `scratch.txt` stands out as left behind, never swept in). To see that
set *before* committing, run `jigc task finalize <id> --dry-run`: it prints the
manifest and stops, changing nothing. A change staged *before* the task existed
refuses to ride the commit (`finalize.carried-staged`) unless you declare it
with `--carry-staged`.

Changed your mind? **`jigc task discard <id>`** abandons the task — it removes
only the working area under `.jigc/tasks/`; no commit is made and the committed
store is untouched. The full reconcile/back-out ladder (the migration review
hold, the carryover gate, the hook rejection above, out-of-band edits) is in
MIGRATING.md → Reconciling and backing out.

**What lands in your repo:** finalize promotes each managed doc under the
**`docs-root`** parent (default `docs/`) at its doctype's location —
`docs/decisions/` (ADRs), `docs/specs/`, `docs/prds/`, `docs/architecture/`
(arch-docs), `docs/milestone-records/` — as plain, human-reviewable Markdown
alongside your own `src/`. (The names are chosen for readability, not a uniform
`<type>s/` rule.) A few doctypes are **placed** rather than located: they live at
one literal path that `docs-root` does not move — the changelog is your
repo-root `CHANGELOG.md` (design/storage.md → Placement).
Prefer a different parent, or the old flat repo-root layout? Set
`jigc config set docs-root <path>` (`.` or `""` for the old flat layout). Everything else jigc
writes lives under `.jigc/` (committed config + bootstrap; gitignored caches) —
see design/storage.md → Repository layout / Config layout. If
you already have a same-named dir (say an existing `docs/architecture/`), run
`jigc ingest` first — it detects and routes existing content rather than
overwriting it.

You can preview part of what finalize will gate on at any time — this task's
content findings, the carryover gate, and the `owner-artifact` causes that need
no staging. The staged set, promotion and the commit itself (your hooks
included) are decided at `finalize`, so a clean `validate` means *nothing this
side of the commit blocks it*, not *this will commit*:

```sh
jigc task validate <id>
jigc task diff <id>
```

---

That is the whole loop: **`jigc setup`** once, then **`jigc start "<intent>"` →
pick from the menu → `jigc start --workflow <chosen> "<intent>"` → implement →
`jigc task finalize <id>`** per task. See
`design/worked-examples.md` for end-to-end flows
and `implementation/roadmap.md` for the build
sequence.
# Migrating to jigc — field notes

Two different migrations get called "migrating to jigc." Both have now been run for real on a brownfield repo (the RC adoption trial, 2026-07-09 → 07-12); these notes distill what worked and what bites. They are working notes, not polished docs — updated as trials land.

1. **Adopting an existing project** — foreign docs (a `.planning/` tree, loose Markdown, an old spec system) become jigc-managed docs. Verb: `jigc ingest` to classify, `jigc migrate <path> --as <doctype>` per doc.
2. **Upgrading a jigc corpus across versions** — committed managed docs move to a new doctype schema-version. Verb: `jigc migrate-corpus`.

## Adopting an existing project

The full method write-up from the reference migration (220 foreign files → 41 managed docs, ~55 commits, one day) is archived at completions/artifacts/RC-adoption/rerun-rc4/migration-method.md. The short version:

1. **Triage with the tool first.** `jigc ingest` classifies every candidate against the managed schemas before you decide anything. Conformant-but-misplaced docs can be adopted; everything else is a re-authoring job through the write verbs. Knowing the split up front sets the whole plan's cost.
2. **Treat every claim in the old docs as unverified.** This is the load-bearing rule, and it is why adoption is a *verification* job, not a reformatting job. Your existing docs may already be lying about the code — status claims especially ("shipped", "passes audit", "the gate works"). Check each claim against the code before carrying it over; a false claim migrated into jigc is *worse* than a deleted one, because the new system lends it credibility (managed, validated, green). Don't migrate what you haven't verified — and where a claim can't be cheaply verified, either drop it or carry it explicitly marked as unverified and put the verification question to the human.
3. **Mine history for the four things worth keeping:** design decisions whose rationale isn't recoverable from the code, still-open debt, architecture knowledge, and work claimed complete that the code doesn't support. Everything else (plan summaries, validation reports, velocity tables) is process exhaust — drop it.
4. **Put the genuine forks to the human** — not "should I proceed" but the actual decisions (delete vs mine-then-delete, is this doc still live, where does the backlog land).
5. **Draft in parallel, write strictly sequentially.** Prose drafting and code-verification parallelize. Since rc.8 the *draft/author* half of bulk migration parallelizes even for docs sharing a directory: two same-directory sources whose slugs would collide today mint **distinct** task ids (a `blake3` of each source path is folded into the migration task id), so their `.jigc/tasks/<id>/` working areas no longer race the tool state. The jigc *writes* still run strictly sequentially — the git-index race is unchanged, each doc mints its own commit, so the finalize/commit path is one process, never parallel.
6. **Author in dependency order.** Cross-referencing docs must land after their targets: ADRs before the arch-docs that cite them — finalize blocks a citation to a doc that doesn't exist.
7. **Let `jigc migrate` retire each source in the same commit as its promoted doc.** The old tree drains itself; there is never a window where content exists in neither place. Then sweep for what the migration broke *outside* the corpus (READMEs pointing at the deleted tree, a stale CLAUDE.md).
8. **Prefer block scalars (`key: |`) in author payloads** for any multi-paragraph prose (the templates demonstrate this since rc.5; double-quoted YAML folds newlines).

## Upgrading a jigc corpus across versions

Verified on the first real committed-corpus upgrade (rc.4 → rc.5, a 41-doc corpus, one doctype with an enum rename across 41 entries — byte-stable, zero prose touched, idempotent re-run). That trial found the *routing* around the upgrade silent, so the rc.6 wave hardened it; the steps below are the shipped surface.

1. **Ask `jigc validate` whether you need to migrate — it blocks if you do.** A committed doc below its doctype's current schema-version raises `schema-conformance.schema-version-current`, routed at `jigc migrate-corpus`, and takes the exit code **non-zero**. The discriminator is each doc's own committed `schema-version` stamp, so the answer never depends on when the store was last stamped.
2. **Run `jigc migrate-corpus` first, `jigc setup` second — and the tool now says so.** Over a stale corpus the `store-version.binary-mismatch` advisory routes at `migrate-corpus` first, and re-stamping the store no longer buys a green: `validate` still blocks on the per-doc stamps. Re-stamp with `jigc setup` once the corpus is current (with the corpus current, the advisory drops `migrate-corpus` from its route). *(Before rc.6 the ordering was yours to enforce — a re-stamped store over an unmigrated corpus validated clean.)*
3. **Look first: `jigc migrate-corpus --dry-run`** prints the triage report the run *would* produce and changes nothing — no migrated bytes, no relocation move, no commit. Run the real thing on a clean tree, so the diff is the whole story.
4. **The run lands its own commit.** `migrate-corpus` writes the migration and commits it, pathspec-limited to the paths it migrated (a half-landed migration — rewritten docs beside a removed relocation source, only some of them staged — is the failure mode that closes). `--no-commit` keeps the writes in the working tree instead, to review them or fold them into a larger commit yourself.
5. **Audit what landed.** The transform is deterministic and the triage (`migrated` / `already_current` / `blocked` in `--format json`) tells you exactly what moved; the line accounting should close exactly (every changed line either a `schema-version` stamp or a declared transform). `blocked` docs are first-class output — they need a human or a prose rewrite, never a workaround.

## Reconciling and backing out

Nothing in either migration is destructive until you say so. The gates, in the order you meet them (each verified against the shipped binary):

1. **Look before landing: `jigc task finalize <id> --dry-run`.** It prints the manifest the finalize *would* commit — each path tagged by how it enters (`promoted` / `modified` / `deleted` / `carried-over`) — and stops. Nothing is committed, and on a migration task the forecast needs no `--approve`. It forecasts no green it would refuse: over a state the carryover gate below blocks, the dry-run emits those findings and takes the refusing exit instead of a manifest (declare the carry with `--carry-staged` and it forecasts it, labelled `carried-over`).
2. **A plain finalize on a migration task holds for review.** `jigc task finalize <id>` without `--approve` renders the fidelity diff — the foreign source beside the canonical rewrite — and exits with nothing committed. The rewrite is the agent's; the CLI guarantees structure, never content-faithfulness, so this hold is where you read. **`--approve` is the sole destructive gate:** only the approving re-run writes the canonical doc, retires the foreign source, and commits.
3. **A same-path migration lands `M`, never `D`+`A`.** When the foreign file already sits at the canonical destination (`jigc migrate docs/decisions/use-postgresql.md --as adr` — the common brownfield case), `--approve` rewrites it **in place**: one commit, `M <path>` in the log, nothing retired. Since rc.7 this holds for every doctype, not just singletons.
4. **Pre-task staged changes refuse to ride: the carryover gate.** Minting a task snapshots the git index, and at finalize anything staged *before the task existed* refuses — one blocking `finalize.carried-staged` per carried path — instead of silently riding the task's commit. Unstage it (`git restore --staged -- <path>`) if it is not the task's work, or declare the carry deliberate with `--carry-staged`; the manifest then labels it `carried-over`. On a migration finalize `--carry-staged` composes with `--approve` — two independent declarations. You meet the gate before the commit boundary now: `jigc task validate <id>` and `jigc task finalize <id> --dry-run` run the same probe and refuse the same states, and both take `--carry-staged` as the same declaration.
5. **A rejecting hook refuses the commit, and the message says how to recover.** jigc never passes `--no-verify` — your `pre-commit`/`commit-msg` hooks are policy — so a hook that exits non-zero stops the run and **nothing was committed** (HEAD does not move). What comes back is the hook's own stderr **verbatim**, a sentence naming what survived, and the exact line to re-run: fix the hook's complaint, run that line, and the commit lands. What survives differs per door and the message states *that door's* truth — `jigc task finalize <id>` leaves the task intact with your staged set still staged and HEAD unmoved; `jigc migrate-corpus` leaves the migrated bytes written and staged, and its re-run **lands** them instead of reporting "already current"; a rejected `jigc milestone create` unwound both its record write and its workbench, so nothing of that milestone survives. All nine committing doors carry the frame, each with its own error code in the invocation log, so a failed run is identifiable afterwards.
6. **Back out a task: `jigc task discard <id>`.** Workbench-only — it removes the task's working area (`.jigc/tasks/<id>/`) and touches nothing else: no commit, the committed store exactly as it was. A migration task discarded before `--approve` leaves the foreign source committed and untouched — abandoning costs nothing.
7. **Back out a milestone: `jigc milestone discard <id>`.** The committed milestone record settles to `status: discarded` in one record-only commit — a genuinely joined sub-task stays `joined`; it really did land — and then the workbench (sub-task areas, fan-out worktrees) tears down. A sub-task worktree holding uncommitted work refuses the discard unless `--force`.
8. **Hand edits are detected and routed — never silently merged, never forbidden.** Editing a committed managed doc outside the loop is expected (it is plain Markdown in git). `jigc validate` names the drifted path with a route to re-author it through the owning workflow; the report is exit-0 at store scope and gates at `jigc task validate` / `jigc task finalize`.

## What migration does *not* give you

- **Truthful prose.** jigc's gates keep docs naming *real code* (anchors, refs, structure); they do not detect that a paragraph's *claim* went stale. A migrated corpus is only as honest as the verification you did at step 2 above — and it starts rotting again the first time a fix lands without its doc pass.
- **A finished doc set.** Migration carries what exists. The gaps the old system had (undocumented decisions, missing specs) are still gaps — now visible ones.

title: Bounding unbounded series cardinality in the sample store
sections:
  - id: question
    set:
      question: |
        <<How do comparable time-series and metrics systems bound unbounded series
        cardinality, and what does each approach cost in return — memory, rejected
        writes, operational complexity, or money?

        `MemoryStore` (`src/store.ts`) keys a `Map<string, Sample[]>` by series
        name. `maxPerSeries` bounds samples *within* one series bucket, and
        `prune(before)` (called from `tick()` against `retentionMs`) evicts a
        bucket once every sample in it has aged out — but nothing bounds how many
        distinct series keys the map holds at once. A caller that folds an
        unbounded-cardinality value into the series name — a user id, a UUID, a
        request id — mints a fresh map entry per distinct value. Each one survives
        for the full retention window (24h by default) before `prune` can remove
        it, so the map's size in that window is bounded only by however many
        distinct series a misbehaving client can generate, not by any limit this
        service imposes. The question: how do systems that solved this problem
        before us bound it, and which cost were they willing to pay to do so?>>
  - id: findings
    set:
      findings: |
        <<Every comparable system answers this with a hard limit somewhere — none
        of them let the series set grow unbounded and rely on later cleanup the
        way pinegrove currently does. They differ in *where* the limit sits and
        *what* it costs.

        **Reject at the edge, keyed by the thing that's actually unbounded.**
        Prometheus, InfluxDB, and Mimir all enforce their cap at write time, not
        as a storage-layer eviction policy. Prometheus's `sample_limit` rejects an
        entire scrape once a target's series count exceeds it; InfluxDB's
        `max-series-per-database` and `max-values-per-tag` reject writes past the
        configured ceiling; Mimir enforces a per-tenant in-memory series cap
        (commonly ~150,000) at the ingester. The common shape: refuse the write
        that would create the Nth-plus-one series, rather than admit it and evict
        something else later. Pinegrove's `IngestQueue` already drops *samples*
        under pressure (oldest-first); none of these systems' cardinality limits
        work that way — they drop the *new series*, not old data, because an
        already-admitted series represents a real thing being measured and a
        rejected-at-birth series (e.g. a runaway UUID label) usually represents
        the bug itself.

        **The cost of not having a limit is measured in real incidents.**
        Prometheus has no default series cap — protection is opt-in — and the
        memory cost is concrete: roughly 3KB per series in the head, so 500K
        active series runs ~1.5GB before any query load, and multi-million-series
        deployments have been observed using 19GB+ for series storage alone.
        Documented failures include a cluster that reached 960GB before OOM
        (1,200 ServiceMonitors feeding it) and WAL-replay crash-loops after
        ingesting a burst of high-cardinality ephemeral metrics. InfluxDB's
        `inmem` series index is the historically-cited reason it earned "the
        cardinality problem" as its signature weakness — every tag value with
        unbounded range (UUID, hash) is memory spent permanently, and its own
        cardinality-limit enforcement has shipped with bugs (the two limits
        interacting incorrectly, cardinality counts going stale once a limit
        trips). A cap is not free either — Mimir's split between "in-memory
        series" (what the limit actually protects) and "active series" (the
        billing-facing number) is itself a recurring source of operator
        confusion.

        **Cost can be pushed onto the caller instead of the operator.**
        Datadog answers the same problem at the business layer: a "custom
        metric" is billed per unique (name, host, tag-combination), so
        cardinality growth becomes a direct, combinatorial dollar cost the
        *customer* absorbs rather than a capacity problem Datadog's own
        infrastructure must solve. Documented cases: one org found its costliest
        metrics carried ~200K cardinality (~$100K/yr once cleaned up); a
        container-id × user-id tag combination on one metric name can reach ~20M
        series (~$1M/month). This doesn't remove the underlying problem — it
        relocates who pays for it, and makes the cost visible and attributable in
        a way an internal memory limit is not.

        **Multi-tenancy turns a global cap into a blast-radius problem.**
        Cortex/Mimir's per-tenant limits exist specifically so one noisy source
        can't exhaust a cap shared by everyone else. Pinegrove currently has no
        tenant or source concept at all — a single global series cap (the
        Prometheus/InfluxDB shape) would mean one runaway client can still starve
        every other series of the map's headroom, which single-tenant systems
        accept as a known limitation of that shape.

        **Root-cause mitigation happens upstream of the store, not inside it.**
        Across every system surveyed, the durable fix for a specific bad label is
        preventing the unbounded value from ever becoming part of a series
        identity — Prometheus's `metric_relabel_configs` to drop or bucket a
        label before ingestion is the clearest example. A store-side cap protects
        the process from dying; it does not, by itself, fix a client that is
        misusing series names as a high-cardinality dimension. Both matter, and
        they are different pieces of work.

        **Gap, not a finding:** LRU/TTL eviction of cold series (evict the
        least-recently-touched series once at a cap, rather than reject new ones)
        and sketch-based cardinality estimation (HyperLogLog, for monitoring
        cardinality itself rather than bounding it) both came up in passing —
        VictoriaMetrics documents `-storage.maxHourlySeries` /

        cite with confidence. Worth a follow-up look before ruling either
        approach in or out.>>

# Bounding unbounded series cardinality in the sample store

## Question

How do comparable time-series and metrics systems bound unbounded series
cardinality, and what does each approach cost in return — memory, rejected
writes, operational complexity, or money?

`MemoryStore` (`src/store.ts`) keys a `Map<string, Sample[]>` by series
name. `maxPerSeries` bounds samples *within* one series bucket, and
`prune(before)` (called from `tick()` against `retentionMs`) evicts a
bucket once every sample in it has aged out — but nothing bounds how many
distinct series keys the map holds at once. A caller that folds an
unbounded-cardinality value into the series name — a user id, a UUID, a
request id — mints a fresh map entry per distinct value. Each one survives
for the full retention window (24h by default) before `prune` can remove
it, so the map's size in that window is bounded only by however many
distinct series a misbehaving client can generate, not by any limit this
service imposes. The question: how do systems that solved this problem
before us bound it, and which cost were they willing to pay to do so?

## Findings

Every comparable system answers this with a hard limit somewhere — none
of them let the series set grow unbounded and rely on later cleanup the
way pinegrove currently does. They differ in *where* the limit sits and
*what* it costs.

**Reject at the edge, keyed by the thing that's actually unbounded.**
Prometheus, InfluxDB, and Mimir all enforce their cap at write time, not
as a storage-layer eviction policy. Prometheus's `sample_limit` rejects an
entire scrape once a target's series count exceeds it; InfluxDB's
`max-series-per-database` and `max-values-per-tag` reject writes past the
configured ceiling; Mimir enforces a per-tenant in-memory series cap
(commonly ~150,000) at the ingester. The common shape: refuse the write
that would create the Nth-plus-one series, rather than admit it and evict
something else later. Pinegrove's `IngestQueue` already drops *samples*
under pressure (oldest-first); none of these systems' cardinality limits
work that way — they drop the *new series*, not old data, because an
already-admitted series represents a real thing being measured and a
rejected-at-birth series (e.g. a runaway UUID label) usually represents
the bug itself.

**The cost of not having a limit is measured in real incidents.**
Prometheus has no default series cap — protection is opt-in — and the
memory cost is concrete: roughly 3KB per series in the head, so 500K
active series runs ~1.5GB before any query load, and multi-million-series
deployments have been observed using 19GB+ for series storage alone.
Documented failures include a cluster that reached 960GB before OOM
(1,200 ServiceMonitors feeding it) and WAL-replay crash-loops after
ingesting a burst of high-cardinality ephemeral metrics. InfluxDB's
`inmem` series index is the historically-cited reason it earned "the
cardinality problem" as its signature weakness — every tag value with
unbounded range (UUID, hash) is memory spent permanently, and its own
cardinality-limit enforcement has shipped with bugs (the two limits
interacting incorrectly, cardinality counts going stale once a limit
trips). A cap is not free either — Mimir's split between "in-memory
series" (what the limit actually protects) and "active series" (the
billing-facing number) is itself a recurring source of operator
confusion.

**Cost can be pushed onto the caller instead of the operator.**
Datadog answers the same problem at the business layer: a "custom
metric" is billed per unique (name, host, tag-combination), so
cardinality growth becomes a direct, combinatorial dollar cost the
*customer* absorbs rather than a capacity problem Datadog's own
infrastructure must solve. Documented cases: one org found its costliest
metrics carried ~200K cardinality (~$100K/yr once cleaned up); a
container-id × user-id tag combination on one metric name can reach ~20M
series (~$1M/month). This doesn't remove the underlying problem — it
relocates who pays for it, and makes the cost visible and attributable in
a way an internal memory limit is not.

**Multi-tenancy turns a global cap into a blast-radius problem.**
Cortex/Mimir's per-tenant limits exist specifically so one noisy source

We bet on a hard, configurable cap on the number of distinct series the
store will hold, enforced at ingest by rejecting the write that would mint
a brand-new series once the cap is reached — while continuing to accept
samples for every series already known. This is the "reject at the edge"
shape the research found dominant across Prometheus's `sample_limit`,
InfluxDB's `max-series-per-database`, and Mimir's per-tenant ingester
cap: refuse the write that would create series N+1, rather than admit it
and evict something else to make room.

We are choosing this over eviction (LRU/TTL of cold series) as the
primary defense, because an evicted series silently drops a real,
already-admitted signal a caller was measuring, while a rejected-at-birth
series is — in the overwhelming common case the research surfaced — the
runaway label itself: a UUID, a user id, a request id folded into a
series name by mistake or by a misbehaving client. Protecting existing
series from a newcomer is a better default than protecting newcomers from
each other.

We are explicitly not betting on, for now:

- **A billing/cost model** (Datadog's answer). Pinegrove has no customers
  to price cardinality to; a dollar cost only works as a limiter when
  someone is paying it.
- **Per-tenant or per-source limits** (Mimir's answer). Pinegrove has no
  tenant or source concept today — one global cap is the only shape that
  fits the current deployment (single process, no multi-tenant callers).
  Revisit if that changes; see open questions.
- **Upstream relabeling** (Prometheus's `metric_relabel_configs`
  equivalent). Pinegrove doesn't own what callers name their series, and
  has no config layer between a caller and `/samples` today. The store
  can protect itself; it can't fix a client's naming scheme.

This keeps the shape consistent with what the store already does at its
other two pressure points — `IngestQueue` drops the oldest *queued*
sample under overflow rather than blocking, and `MemoryStore.put` drops
the oldest *stored* sample once a series bucket is full rather than
growing it — both protect the process by shedding load at a hard,
configured boundary instead of letting a structure grow without limit.

#### Proves

A caller can drive the store to its configured series cap and
no further: seeding the cap's worth of distinct series and then
sending one more, previously-unseen series is rejected with a
loud, distinguishable signal — while every one of the already-
admitted series keeps accepting new samples without
interruption or eviction. `store.size()` / `store.series()`
after the attempt shows exactly the cap's worth of series, never
more, and none of the pre-existing series lost a sample to make
room. This proves the actual bet from VISION.md: the process
cannot be grown past a bounded memory footprint by cardinality
alone, and a caller can tell the difference between "your
payload was malformed" and "the store is full of series."

**Increment 1 — cap enforcement in the store.** Add
`maxSeries` to `Config` (`ROLLUP_MAX_SERIES`, following
`ROLLUP_MAX_SAMPLES`'s existing `readPositiveInt` pattern) and
thread it into `MemoryStore`'s constructor alongside
`maxPerSeries`. In `put`, when the sample's series is not
already a key in `buckets` and `buckets.size` has reached

a sample for an existing series is never affected. This is the
whole of the OOM protection the vision bets on — the riskiest

# Reject a new series at the cap rather than evicting to make room

## Context

`MemoryStore`'s `buckets` map (`src/store.ts`) is keyed by series name and
was unbounded in key count — `maxPerSeries` only ever bounded a single
bucket's length. `VISION.md` commits to a hard, configurable cap on
distinct series, enforced at ingest, chosen over cold-series eviction as
the primary defense (an evicted series silently drops real signal; a
rejected-at-birth series is, in the common case the research surfaced, the
runaway label itself). This ADR is the concrete implementation of that bet
inside `MemoryStore.put`.

## Options



## Decision

`MemoryStore` now takes a `maxSeries` constructor argument alongside
`maxPerSeries`. In `put`, a sample for a series not already in `buckets`
is refused — the bucket is never created — once `buckets.size` has
reached `maxSeries`; a sample for a series already present is always
admitted, regardless of how full the store is. `put`'s signature changes
from `void` to `boolean`: `true` when the sample was admitted, `false`
when it was refused for cardinality. `Config` gains a matching
`maxSeries` field, read from `ROLLUP_MAX_SERIES` with the same
`readPositiveInt` validation as the other numeric config keys, defaulting
to a placeholder value of `10_000` pending the measured default the
deferral ledger owes. `Router.ingest`'s accepted-count now reflects
`put`'s return value instead of assuming every call succeeded, but no new
error type or distinct response status is introduced yet — that is the
next sub-task's job.

## Consequences

The store can no longer be grown past a bounded number of distinct series
by cardinality alone — the core protection the milestone exists to
deliver. The cost: a caller whose write is refused for cardinality
currently sees the same outcome as if the line were silently dropped
(the accepted count just comes back lower than the line count, with no
distinct signal) — `Router.ingest` doesn't yet expose *why* a line wasn't
counted. That gap is deliberate and scoped to the next sub-task
(`give-the-series-cap-rejection`), which gives cardinality rejection its
own error type and a distinguishable response, per the decisions log.
Every existing call site constructing `MemoryStore` or reading `put`'s
return value needed updating for the new signature; there were only two
(`src/index.ts`, `test/rollup.test.ts`), both updated here.

Going back through the transcript honestly:

**1. What confused me**

The biggest one: the milestone sub-task resume text (`jigc start --task add-a-configurable-rollup-max`) printed explicit instructions to author commit prose — `jigc doc set-field commit:add-a-configurable-rollup-max#type --value <COMMIT_TYPE> ...` — as if a per-sub-task `commit` doc existed and I owned it. It doesn't apply cleanly in that context (see #2). I also got confused by `jigc start --task <sub-task-id>` refusing outright right after minting: `task is pinned to base a99b6d9 but you're on 1d46b86` — the milestone's own bookkeeping commits (`chore(milestone): record task:...`) had already moved HEAD past the sub-task's pin, so the very act of seeding two sub-tasks made both un-resumable from the main tree. Nothing up to that point told me sub-tasks need `jigc milestone provision` + working from `.jigc/worktrees/<id>` — I only learned it from the error text. And I couldn't build a confident mental model of how `jigc milestone finalize` combines *code* (not just docs) across independent sub-task worktrees when two increments are code-dependent rather than parallel/disjoint — more on that in #3 and #4.

**2. What jigc told me that turned out wrong or misleading**

The sub-task instructions telling me to `jigc doc set-field commit:<task-id>#type ...` and "Author this sub-task's own commit prose" were simply inapplicable: trying it gave `create.gate-blocked` — `the workflow does not allow jigc doc create commit in-task; allowed doctypes: [adr]`. So the printed steps described an action the tool then refused. I never found this reconciled anywhere; I inferred (from the eventual `milestone finalize` output showing a CLI-synthesized `subject: "Finalize milestone ... (2 sub-tasks)"`) that commit-message authorship is a milestone-level concern, not a sub-task-level one, but the composed task text never said that — it just handed me commands that didn't work.

Also mildly misleading: `jigc milestone join --help` describes the operation purely as a "disjoint-union" of "staged docs." That description says nothing about code. It was only from the *sub-task instructions* ("git add your code edits so the milestone can fold this worktree's staged index") and later the actual `finalize` output (`"code_files": 7`) that I learned code folding is real and separate from the doc-join. The `--help` text for the verb that actually does the work undersold what it does.

**3. What I looked for and didn't find**

- A dry-run for `jigc milestone finalize`. `jigc task finalize` has `--dry-run`; the milestone equivalent doesn't, per its `--help`. Given finalize is the one-shot commit boundary and I was uncertain how it would treat two worktrees with overlapping code changes, I wanted to preview it and couldn't.
- Any explanation of how sub-task worktrees' *code* diffs combine at finalize when they're not independent — nothing in `--help`, `jigc describe`, or (per AGENT.md's own instruction to ask the binary, not a source tree) anywhere I could reach explained the merge semantics for dependent/overlapping diffs across sub-task worktrees.
- A focused `jigc describe <item>` — I tried `jigc describe milestone` hoping for a targeted explanation; it errored (`unexpected argument 'milestone' found`). `describe` only does the full tour or category flags, not a single-item lookup.

**4. What I did around jigc instead of through it**

- `git reset --hard a99b6d9` directly on the `add-a-configurable-rollup-max` worktree, to discard its staged code. I made this call because increment 2 genuinely depends on increment 1's code (same functions in `store.ts`/`router.ts`), the two sub-task worktrees start as independent detached checkouts of the same base with no jigc-sanctioned way to layer one sub-task's in-progress code onto another's, and there was no dry-run to test the dependent case safely first. Rather than risk `jigc milestone finalize` on an untested overlapping-diff scenario, I used plain git to consolidate all code into one worktree and reset the other to clean, then let `join`/`finalize` run over a case I actually understood.
- To confirm that was safe, I inspected jigc's internal storage directly — `cat .gitignore`, `git check-ignore -v .jigc/tasks .jigc/worktrees .jigc/milestones`, and checked for a per-worktree `.jigc/tasks` directory — to verify a sub-task's in-flight doc content (the ADR) lives centrally under the gitignored `.jigc/tasks/`, not in the worktree's git-tracked files, so resetting the worktree's code wouldn't blow away the ADR I'd already authored through jigc. That's investigation of jigc's own plumbing via the filesystem/git rather than asking the tool, done only because no `jigc` verb surfaced that guarantee.

I didn't read or hand-edit any *managed doc* content directly — all doc writes went through `jigc doc` verbs — but the worktree reset and the storage-layout probing are real workarounds, not sanctioned jigc paths.
